title: Necklace Divisor-Sum Form: ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d = (#necklaces)·n
description: Pushes the parent's rotation-indexed cyclic Burnside count ∑_{r:ZMod n} k^{gcd(n,r)} = (#necklaces up to rotation)·n into the classical divisor-sum form ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d, answering the parent entry's openQuestions[1] verbatim. The bridge is a pure number-theoretic reindexing of the rotation sum, independent of the necklace interpretation: (A) the rotation sum over ZMod n equals the range sum over {0,…,n−1} via the bijection r ↦ r.val (sum_zmod_eq_sum_range); (B) the range sum equals the divisor sum by grouping the integers i < n according to gcd(n,i), whose fibre over each divisor d has exactly φ(n/d) elements (Mathlib's totient_div_of_dvd) and on which the summand is the constant k^d, assembled by fiberwise summation (sum_range_pow_gcd_eq_divisor_sum); (C) combining (A), (B) with the parent's sum_pow_gcd_eq_card_necklaces_mul gives the classical necklace identity ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d = (#necklaces)·n (divisor_sum_eq_card_necklaces_mul), so dividing by n recovers the textbook formula (1/n)∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d) k^d; (D) the symmetric d ↔ n/d reindexing gives the equivalent form ∑_{d∣n} φ(d)·k^{n/d} (divisor_sum_symm, symm_divisor_sum_eq_card_necklaces_mul).

divisor_sum_eq_card_necklaces_mul (C): ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d = (#necklaces up to rotation)·n, closing the gap between the parent's gcd-indexed sum and the divisor-sum form quoted in every reference statement of the cyclic necklace theorem

overview.historicalContext: The textbook formula for the number of k-colored necklaces of n beads up to rotation is (1/n)·∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d (equivalently (1/n)·∑_{d∣n} φ(d)·k^{n/d}), a direct application of Burnside's lemma to the cyclic group. The standard derivation groups the n rotations by their order: there are exactly φ(n/d) rotations whose cycle structure consists of d cycles, each fixing k^d colorings. The parent gallery entry burnside-counting-oq-03-oq-02-oq-01 proved the rotation-indexed form ∑_{r:ZMod n} k^{gcd(n,r)} = (#necklaces)·n and explicitly flagged (openQuestions[1]) the remaining step: push this sum into the classical divisor form by grouping rotations of the same order. This entry supplies that bridge as a pure number-theoretic reindexing, completing the classical necklace-counting identity in the gallery.
overview.problemStatement: Starting from the parent's rotation-indexed cyclic Burnside count ∑_{r:ZMod n} k^{gcd(n,r)} = (#necklaces up to rotation)·n, prove the classical divisor-sum form ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d = (#necklaces)·n, and its symmetric variant ∑_{d∣n} φ(d)·k^{n/d} = (#necklaces)·n, so that dividing by n recovers the textbook necklace formula.
overview.proofStrategy:
**(A) Rotation sum = range sum.** The map r ↦ r.val is a bijection ZMod n ≃ {0,…,n−1}, with inverse i ↦ (i : ZMod n) (membership via ZMod.val_lt and Finset.mem_range; the round trips via ZMod.natCast_zmod_val and ZMod.val_natCast_of_lt). Finset.sum_bij' transports ∑_{r:ZMod n} k^{gcd(n,r.val)} to ∑_{i<n} k^{gcd(n,i)}.

**(B) Range sum = divisor sum.** The function g i = gcd(n,i) maps range n into n.divisors (gcd(n,i) ∣ n and n ≠ 0). Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to' regroups ∑_{i<n} k^{gcd(n,i)} as ∑_{d∣n} ∑_{i<n, gcd(n,i)=d} k^d. On each fibre the summand k^d is constant (Finset.sum_const, smul_eq_mul) and the fibre has φ(n/d) elements (Nat.totient_div_of_dvd, valid for d ∣ n), giving ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d.

**(C) Necklace count.** Chain (A) and (B) backwards and apply the parent's sum_pow_gcd_eq_card_necklaces_mul, yielding ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d = Nat.card (orbitRel.Quotient (Rot n) (Rot n → Fin k))·n.

**(D) Symmetric form.** Nat.sum_div_divisors rewrites ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d as ∑_{d∣n} of the same summand at n/d; Nat.div_div_self (for d ∣ n, n ≠ 0) collapses n/(n/d) = d, producing ∑_{d∣n} φ(d)·k^{n/d}. Composing with (C) gives the symmetric necklace identity (D′).
keyInsights: **The divisor form is pure number theory.** The passage from the gcd-indexed rotation sum to ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d needs no necklace or group input — it is a reindexing of ∑_{i<n} k^{gcd(n,i)} by the level sets of gcd(n,·), so the entire bridge factors through Finset.sum_bij' and Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to'.

**The fibre count is exactly the totient.** The number of i < n with gcd(n,i) = d is φ(n/d) (Mathlib's totient_div_of_dvd); this single fact converts the fiberwise sum of the constant k^d into the textbook coefficient φ(n/d) and is the crux of the whole identity.

**ZMod n ≃ range n decouples indexing from algebra.** Summing over the rotation group ZMod n and summing over {0,…,n−1} are interchangeable via r ↦ r.val, so the parent's algebraically-stated count and the number-theorist's range sum are literally the same number.

**Symmetry is free reindexing.** The two equivalent textbook forms ∑φ(n/d)k^d and ∑φ(d)k^{n/d} differ only by the involution d ↔ n/d on the divisor set (Nat.sum_div_divisors, Nat.div_div_self), so neither is more fundamental — the count is symmetric under it.

overview.what: The classical divisor-sum form of the cyclic necklace count: ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d = (#necklaces up to rotation)·n, equivalently ∑_{d∣n} φ(d)·k^{n/d} = (#necklaces)·n, so the number of k-colored n-bead necklaces is (1/n)·∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d) k^d.

sections.title: Section A: Rotation Sum = Range Sum

conclusion.summary: Pushes the parent's rotation-indexed cyclic Burnside count into the classical divisor-sum form by a pure number-theoretic reindexing: (A) ∑_{r:ZMod n} = ∑_{i<n} via r ↦ r.val (Finset.sum_bij'), (B) ∑_{i<n} k^{gcd(n,i)} = ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d by grouping i < n on the level sets of gcd(n,·) (Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to', Nat.totient_div_of_dvd), (C) ∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d)·k^d = (#necklaces)·n via the parent's count, and (D) the symmetric ∑_{d∣n} φ(d)·k^{n/d} form by the d ↔ n/d involution. conclusion.implications: Completes the classical cyclic necklace-counting theorem in the gallery: the number of k-colored n-bead necklaces up to rotation is (1/n)·∑_{d∣n} φ(n/d) k^d = (1/n)·∑_{d∣n} φ(d) k^{n/d}, both derived as specializations of the parent's verified Burnside average. It shows the bridge from the group-theoretic orbit count to the φ-weighted divisor sum is a clean reindexing requiring no further group theory.
